Calculate the standard cell potential in (V) of the cell in which following reaction takes place :

Fe2+(aq) + Ag+(aq) $$ \to $$ Fe3+(aq) + Ag (s)

Given that

$$E_{A{g^ + }/Ag}^o = xV$$

$$E_{Fe^{2+ }/Fe}^o = yV$$

questions.explanation:
Standard emf,


${E^0} = E_{A{g^ + }|Ag}^0 - E_{F{e^{3 + }}|F{e^{2 + }}}^0$$  ..............(1)


Given $$E_{Fe^{2+ }/Fe}^o = yV$$


$$ \therefore $$ Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> $$ \to $$ Fe ..........(2)


${E^0}$$ = y and $$\Delta {G^0}$$ = -2Fy


Also given $$E_{Fe^{3+ }/Fe}^o = zV$$


$$ \therefore $$ Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>-</sup> $$ \to $$ Fe .........(3)


${E^0}$$ = z and $$\Delta {G^0}$$ = -3Fz


Performing (2) - (1), we get


 Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> $$ \to $$ Fe<sup>2+</sup>


$$ \therefore $$ $$\Delta {G^0}$$ = -3Fz + 2Fy


$$ \Rightarrow $$ -(1)F${E^0}$$ = -3Fz + 2Fy


$$ \therefore $$ $$E_{F{e^{3 + }}|F{e^{2 + }}}^0$$ = 3z - 2y


From Equation (1),


${E^0} = E_{A{g^ + }|Ag}^0 - E_{F{e^{3 + }}|F{e^{2 + }}}^0$$


= x - (3z - 2y) = x + 2y - 3z

kinetic energy(KE) of ejected

= $$\sqrt {{{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^N {{{\left( {{x_i} - \overline x } \right)}^2}} } \over N}} $$


= $$\sqrt {{\matrix{
  {\left( {45 - 48} \right)^2} + {\left( {54 - 48} \right)^2} \hfill \cr 
   + {\left( {41 - 48} \right)^2} + {\left( {57 - 48} \right)^2} \hfill \cr 
   + {\left( {43 - 48} \right)^2} + {\left( {48 - 48} \right)^2} \hfill \cr}  \over 6}} $$


= $$\sqrt {{{9 + 36 + 49 + 81 + 25} \over 6}} $$


= $$\sqrt {{{200} \over 6}} $$


= $$\sqrt {{{100} \over 3}} $$


= ${{10} \over {\sqrt 3 }}$$

put log<sub>10</sub> x = t

questions.question:
If surface tension (S), Moment of inertia (I) and
Planck's constant (h), were to be taken as the
fundamental units, the dimensional formula for
linear momentum would be :-
questions.explanation:
We know,


surface tension (S) = ${F \over L}$$ = ${{\left[ {ML{T^{ - 2}}} \right]} \over {\left[ L \right]}}$$


$$ \therefore $$ [S] = ${\left[ {M{T^{ - 2}}} \right]}$$


Moment of inertia (I) = mr<sup>2</sup>


$$ \therefore $$ [I] = ${\left[ {M{L^2}} \right]}$$


Planck's constant (h) = ${E \over f}$$ = Et


$$ \therefore $$ [h] = ${\left[ {M{L^2}{T^{ - 1}}} \right]}$$


Also linear momentum (p) = mv = ${\left[ {ML{T^{ - 1}}} \right]}$$


Now we have to express p in terms of s, I and h.


$$ \therefore $$ Let, [P] = [S<sup>a</sup> I<sup>b</sup> h<sup>c</sup>]


$$ \Rightarrow $$ ${\left[ {ML{T^{ - 1}}} \right]}$$ = ${\left[ {M{T^{ - 2}}} \right]}$$<sup>a</sup> ${\left[ {M{L^2}} \right]}$$<sup>b</sup> ${\left[ {M{L^2}{T^{ - 1}}} \right]}$$<sup>c</sup>


$$ \Rightarrow $$ ${\left[ {ML{T^{ - 1}}} \right]}$$ = [ M<sup>a + b + c</sup> L<sup>2b +2c</sup> T<sup>- 2a - c</sup> ]


By comparing the dimensions of both sides, we get


a + b + c = 1  .........(1)


2b +2c = 1  ..............(2)


- 2a - c = -1   ...................(3)


By solving those three equations we get,


a = ${1 \over 2}$$


b = ${1 \over 2}$$


c = 0


$$ \therefore $$  linear momentum [p] = [S<sup>1/2</sup>I<sup>1/2</sup>h<sup>0</sup>]
